title: Pulse and Glide Driving Technique Explained With Automatic Transmission: Engineering Telemetry & Protocol
description: Master the pulse and glide driving technique with an automatic transmission. Learn how to optimize BSFC, manage torque converters, and gain 15% to 25% MPG.
author: TN Tayyab
authorCredentials: Senior Automotive Diagnostic Engineer & Eco-Driving Specialist
directAnswer: Pulse-and-glide in an automatic hybrid involves briskly accelerating to 40 mph at peak thermal engine efficiency, then lifting the throttle completely to enter zero-fuel electrical freewheeling down to 30 mph. Drivers operating traditional torque-converter automatics achieve 15% to 22% fuel economy gains by applying 70% to 80% throttle during the pulse phase to leverage the engine's optimal Brake Specific Fuel Consumption (BSFC) sweet spot, followed by gentle throttle feathering to initiate Deceleration Fuel Cut-Off (DFCO) or safe neutral freewheeling. In conventional automatic transmissions, shifting into neutral while rolling preserves kinetic momentum by preventing transmission drag, provided the transmission utilizes an engine-driven mechanical oil pump. In Toyota and Lexus power-split hybrids (e-CVT), pulse-and-glide eliminates mechanical pumping losses entirely by entering the electric 'stealth glide' mode, where the engine shuts off and planetary gear electric motors cancel regenerative drag. Mastering this cycle delivers significant fuel reductions without impeding traffic flow.
keyTakeaways: The 15% to 25% Fuel Economy Gain: Pulse-and-glide yields a measured 15% to 22% MPG gain in conventional automatic transmissions and a 25% to 38% MPG gain in power-split hybrid automatics.

The BSFC Thermodynamic Foundation: Accelerating at 70% to 80% throttle operates internal combustion engines at peak 38% to 41% thermal efficiency, converting more fuel chemical energy into kinetic propulsion.

Traditional Automatic Glide Options: Non-hybrid automatics execute glides via two distinct methods: In-Gear Overdrive DFCO (zero fuel injection but engine braking drag) or Neutral Coasting (engine idles at 0.18 GPH with zero mechanical drag).

Transmission Mechanical Safety: Modern planetary automatic transmissions suffer zero internal lubrication damage when coasting in Neutral with the engine running, because the front transmission pump is driven directly by the engine crankshaft.

The Hybrid e-CVT Super Glide: Hybrids achieve frictionless glides through delicate throttle feathering that balances traction motor torque to zero amps, keeping the gas engine off and regenerative braking deactivated.

sections.heading: The Thermodynamics of Pulse and Glide: Exploiting the BSFC Thermal Sweet Spot
sections.content:
Internal combustion engines operate at maximum thermal efficiency—converting up to 41% of fuel energy into mechanical work—only when operating under moderate-to-heavy throttle loads between 70% and 80% of peak torque. Automotive gasoline engines are notoriously inefficient when driven at a steady suburban speed of 35 or 45 mph. To maintain a constant 35 mph on a level road, an automobile requires only 7 to 10 horsepower. Generating this tiny fraction of engine power forces the throttle butterfly plate almost completely closed.

This closed throttle condition creates a deep intake manifold vacuum of -18 to -22 inHg (30 to 40 kPa absolute pressure). The engine acts as a massive vacuum pump, expending a large portion of its fuel energy simply pulling intake air past the throttled butterfly valve—an engineering loss designated as parasitic pumping work. Under these light-load conditions, Brake Specific Fuel Consumption (BSFC) degrades to an inefficient 320 to 380 grams of fuel per kilowatt-hour (g/kWh), yielding a poor thermal efficiency of only 22% to 25%.

The pulse-and-glide technique resolves this thermodynamic flaw by dividing driving into two distinct phases:

  • The Pulse Phase (Brisk Acceleration): The driver applies 70% to 80% throttle travel, accelerating firmly from 30 to 45 mph. The throttle plate opens wide, eliminating intake vacuum (manifold absolute pressure rises to 85 to 92 kPa). Pumping work drops to near zero, and the engine enters its optimal BSFC thermal sweet spot of 215 to 235 g/kWh at 40% thermal efficiency. The engine converts fuel into forward vehicle kinetic energy (Ek = ½mv²) with maximum mechanical yield.
  • The Glide Phase (Frictionless Momentum Roll): Upon reaching 45 mph, the driver terminates the pulse phase and transitions the vehicle into a freewheeling glide down to 30 mph. During the glide, the engine either shuts off entirely (in hybrids) or burns a minuscule idle fuel rate (0.18 to 0.22 gallons per hour in conventional automatics), while the vehicle travels hundreds of feet using stored kinetic energy alone.

Thermodynamic Fact: It is significantly more fuel-efficient to burn fuel at 40% thermal efficiency for 6 seconds during a pulse and then travel for 20 seconds on zero or idle fuel during a glide, than to burn fuel continuously at 24% thermal efficiency for 26 seconds to maintain an identical average speed.

sections.heading: Automatic Transmission Architectures: Torque Converter, DCT, CVT, and e-CVT
sections.content:
The execution of pulse-and-glide differs fundamentally across automatic transmission architectures due to varying clutch engagement mechanisms and hydraulic pump drives. Understanding your vehicle's specific transmission mechanics determines whether to execute in-gear glides, neutral glides, or electrical freewheel glides:

1. Conventional Planetary Automatics (6-Speed, 8-Speed, 10-Speed)

Traditional automatic transmissions utilize planetary gearsets paired with a hydrodynamic torque converter. The transmission fluid pump (gerotor or crescent pump) is driven directly by the torque converter impeller hub, which bolts mechanically to the engine flexplate. As long as the internal combustion engine is running (even at 650 RPM idle), the hydraulic pump spins, circulating ATF at 60 to 120 PSI of line pressure through the valve body, cooling circuits, and planetary gear bushings. This architecture supports both In-Gear DFCO gliding and Neutral coasting without mechanical lubrication starvation.

2. Dual-Clutch Transmissions (DCT / DSG)

Dual-clutch automatics utilize computer-controlled electro-hydraulic or electromechanical actuators to engage alternating wet or dry clutches. When the driver lifts off the accelerator at highway speeds in vehicles equipped with an active "Eco-Coasting" profile (such as Volkswagen DSG or Porsche PDK), the transmission control unit automatically opens both clutches, decoupling the engine and letting it drop to idle. Drivers without factory coasting software perform in-gear glides to avoid manual shift-lever wear on synchronizer sleeves.

3. Continuously Variable Transmissions (Steel Push-Belt CVT)

Push-belt and chain CVTs (found in Subaru Lineartronic, Nissan Xtronic, and Honda platforms) regulate drive ratios by adjusting hydraulic fluid clamping pressure against cone pulleys. The CVT high-pressure pump is driven directly by the engine crankshaft. When performing pulse-and-glide in a conventional CVT, accelerate firmly to establish pulley clamping, then lift the throttle smoothly to allow the transmission to transition to its tallest virtual overdrive ratio (spanning 0.45:1 to 0.55:1).

4. Power-Split Hybrid Electric Transmissions (Toyota HSD / Ford e-CVT)

Toyota Hybrid Synergy Drive and Ford e-CVT architectures contain zero friction clutches, zero bands, and zero torque converters. They connect the combustion engine, a smaller motor-generator (MG1), and a larger traction motor (MG2) through a single planetary gearset. In this transmission, pulse-and-glide reaches its highest expression: lifting the pedal feather-lightly commands the inverter to deliver zero current to both electric motors while shutting down fuel injection and stopping the gas engine entirely. The vehicle freewheels with zero pumping resistance and zero engine braking.

sections.heading: The Shifting to Neutral Debate: Mechanical Facts vs Myths
sections.content:
Shifting a modern torque-converter automatic transmission into Neutral while rolling at speeds under 45 mph causes zero mechanical damage if the internal combustion engine remains idling. Persistent automotive mythology claims that shifting an automatic transmission into neutral while rolling instantly burns up clutch packs and destroys planetary gearsets. A factual analysis of transmission hydraulic schematics separates mechanical truth from myth:

The Transmission Lubrication Reality

Transmission internal failure occurs only if internal planetary gears rotate while starved of lubrication oil. The automatic transmission fluid pump is mechanically splined to the torque converter housing, which is bolted to the engine crankshaft. As long as the engine idles at 650 to 750 RPM in Neutral, the front pump continuously circulates 12 to 18 liters of pressurized ATF per minute through the transmission cooler and straight into the center lubrication passages of the output shaft. Planetary carrier needle bearings and bushings receive 100% full pressurized oil flow regardless of vehicle road speed.

⚙️ The True Neutral Towing Danger

The myth of transmission damage stems from flat-towing a broken vehicle with the engine turned OFF. When a car is towed with the engine stopped, vehicle wheels spin the transmission output shaft and planetary gears while the engine-driven oil pump remains stationary. In that scenario, dry metal-on-metal friction destroys planetary bushings within 10 miles. Coasting in neutral with the engine running presents zero risk of oil starvation.

DFCO in Drive vs Neutral Coasting: The Physics Trade-Off

Hypermilers debate whether to leave the transmission in "Drive" (triggering Deceleration Fuel Cut-Off, or DFCO) or shift to "Neutral" during a glide:

  • In-Gear DFCO Glide: When the driver lifts off the throttle in Drive, the ECU detects zero throttle angle and engine speed above 1,150 RPM. The ECU cuts fuel injector pulse width to exactly 0.00 milliseconds. Fuel consumption is absolute zero. However, the transmission remains mechanically coupled to the engine, forcing the moving car to spin the engine pistons against compression resistance. This engine braking decelerates the vehicle rapidly, limiting the glide distance to 300 to 450 feet.
  • Neutral Idle Glide: When shifted into Neutral, the engine decouples from the wheels and idles at 650 RPM, consuming a nominal 0.18 gallons per hour (approximately 1.8 milliliters per second). Because engine braking is eliminated, mechanical rolling resistance is drastically lower. The vehicle glides for 1,200 to 1,800 feet before decelerating from 45 to 30 mph—traveling over three times farther on momentum alone.

The mathematical net benefit favors Neutral gliding on long, gentle slopes and flat secondary roadways where extended rolling distance far outweighs the tiny 0.18 GPH idle fuel consumption. For shorter decelerations approaching stop signs or red traffic signals, In-Gear DFCO is superior because fuel burn is zero and engine braking preserves friction brake pads.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step Pulse and Glide Protocol for Traditional Automatics (Torque Converter & CVT)
sections.content:
Executing pulse-and-glide in a non-hybrid automatic transmission requires accelerating at 75% throttle from 30 to 45 mph, followed by clean throttle release into an extended roll. Implement this four-phase operational procedure on flat or gently undulating secondary roadways with minimal surrounding traffic:

Phase 1: Pre-Flight Safety & Traffic Screening

Before initiating pulse-and-glide cycles, scan your mirrors and confirm that no trailing vehicle is closely following your rear bumper. Select a secondary multi-lane road or open rural arterial with a posted speed limit of 40 to 45 mph. Ensure your vehicle engine has reached full operating temperature (engine coolant temperature between 190°F and 205°F / 88°C to 96°C), as cold engines will not lock torque converters or engage DFCO fuel cutoffs.

Phase 2: The High-Efficiency Pulse

From an initial speed of 30 mph, depress the accelerator pedal smoothly and assertively to 70% to 80% throttle travel. Do not stomp the pedal to the floor, as kicking the kickdown switch commands open-loop fuel enrichment. Accelerating at 75% throttle opens the throttle plate, raises manifold pressure to 85 kPa, and forces the transmission to upshift firmly into 3rd, 4th, and 5th gear while locking the torque converter clutch. Continue brisk acceleration until the speedometer reads 45 mph (requiring approximately 5 to 7 seconds).

Phase 3: The Seamless Transition

Upon reaching 45 mph, smoothly lift your right foot completely off the accelerator pedal over a 0.5-second interval. Do not snap your foot off violently, which induces driveline lash. As the throttle valve closes, the transmission control module commands a shift into the highest available overdrive gear (e.g., 8th gear) and closes the injectors into DFCO mode.

Phase 4: The Extended Glide (Method A or Method B)

Select your preferred glide execution method based on roadway topography and traffic conditions:

  • Method A (In-Gear DFCO Glide): Leave the gear selector in "D". Rest your foot lightly on the pedal without depressing it. The vehicle decelerates gradually under mild engine compression braking while consuming zero fuel. When road speed reaches 30 mph, smoothly re-apply 75% throttle to begin the next pulse.
  • Method B (Neutral Glide): With the engine idling, bump the gear selector forward from "D" to "N" (without pressing the shift interlock thumb button). The tachometer drops instantly to 650 RPM idle. The vehicle freewheels with minimal rolling friction, gliding for up to a third of a mile. When speed rolls back to 30 mph, gently tap the accelerator to raise engine RPM to 1,200 (rev-matching), pull the shifter back into "D", and smoothly apply 75% throttle for the subsequent pulse.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step Protocol for Hybrid Automatics: The Toyota & Lexus e-CVT 'Super Glide'
sections.content:
Toyota and Lexus hybrid electronic CVTs achieve the highest pulse-and-glide efficiency by utilizing the hybrid synergy energy monitor to locate the zero-arrows freewheel state. In Toyota Hybrid Synergy Drive (HSD) platforms—including the Prius, Camry Hybrid, RAV4 Hybrid, and Lexus ES300h—the transmission contains no friction clutches or torque converter. In these vehicles, hypermilers execute the legendary "Super Glide" (or electrical neutral freewheel) through delicate pedal modulation:

Step 1: The Engine-Driven Pulse Phase

Accelerate firmly from 28 mph up to 42 mph with the accelerator depressed approximately 50% to 60%, positioning the Eco-gauge needle right at the upper border of the "ECO" zone (immediately below the "POWER" threshold). In this power state, the 2.5L or 1.8L Atkinson-cycle combustion engine operates at its peak thermal efficiency island of 40% to 41% (BSFC 205 g/kWh), directly driving the wheels while generator MG1 routes surplus torque to charge the high-voltage traction battery.

Step 2: The Throttle Lift and Engine Shutdown

At 42 mph, lift your foot completely off the accelerator pedal for one full second. Because road speed is below 46 mph (the internal combustion engine rotation threshold for Gen 3 and Gen 4 Toyota hybrids), the Hybrid Control Module detects zero throttle demand and shuts down fuel injection, completely stopping internal combustion engine crankshaft rotation to 0 RPM.

Step 3: Finding the Zero-Current "Dead Pedal" Position

Once the engine stops, gently depress the accelerator pedal by approximately 5% to 8% travel while observing the Energy Monitor display on your dashboard or center screen. Modulate your foot until all energy flow arrows disappear entirely: no blue arrows from the battery to the electric motor, no green arrows from the wheels regenerating into the battery, and no red arrows from the gas engine. This balanced position delivers exactly zero amps to traction motor MG2, eliminating electromagnetic drag and allowing the vehicle to freewheel with near-zero rolling resistance.

Step 4: Cycling the Super Glide

Maintain this feather-light pedal position as the hybrid glides silently for up to 2,000 feet, bleeding speed gently from 42 mph down to 28 mph. Because the gas engine is stopped (0 RPM) and regenerative braking is suppressed, the car rolls significantly farther than standard EV coasting mode. When velocity drops to 28 mph, press the accelerator firmly back to the upper ECO threshold to begin the next high-efficiency pulse.

⚡ The 46 MPH Hybrid Threshold

In Toyota hybrid systems, planetary gear mechanics dictate that generator MG1 must not exceed 10,000 RPM. Above 46 mph (or 65 mph in Gen 4 and Gen 5 systems), the gas engine must spin without fuel to protect MG1 from overspeeding. Therefore, low-speed pulse-and-glide between 28 and 42 mph achieves the highest efficiency by ensuring true 0-RPM engine shutdown.

sections.heading: Empirical OBD2 CAN-Bus Telemetry: 50-Mile Suburban Route Comparison
sections.content:
A 50-mile comparative suburban test between steady throttle driving and pulse-and-glide in an 8-speed automatic passenger sedan demonstrated an average fuel economy increase of 21.4%. Testing was executed along a flat 10-mile suburban arterial loop with traffic signals timed for 40 mph progression. Ambient air temperature was 72°F (22°C) with calm wind conditions. Three distinct driving protocols were evaluated over 50 miles each in a 2.0L direct-injection automatic sedan (curb weight 3,150 lbs) and a 2.5L hybrid crossover (curb weight 3,650 lbs):

2.0L Auto: In-Gear DFCO Pulse & Glide 36.8 MPH 1.28 Gallons 39.1 MPG 38 Cycles (30 → 45 MPH) +12.7% Fuel Economy

In the non-hybrid automatic sedan, shifting to Neutral during the glide delivered an additional 3.0 MPG over in-gear DFCO gliding. Because the vehicle experienced zero engine compression drag in Neutral, each glide covered an average of 1,420 feet compared to only 480 feet in DFCO mode. The sedan completed the 50-mile course with only 26 pulse events in Neutral versus 38 pulses in DFCO, spending 62% of total route distance with the engine simply idling.

In the hybrid crossover, the Super Glide protocol lifted fuel economy from 51.0 MPG to an astonishing 68.5 MPG—a 34.3% reduction in gasoline consumption. The hybrid covered 24.8 of the 50 test miles with the internal combustion engine completely powered down.

sections.heading: Traffic Etiquette, Brake Wear, and Hypermiling Safety Rules
sections.content:
Pulse-and-glide driving must strictly occur on low-density secondary arterials or multi-lane roadways where velocity cycling does not compress rear following buffers. Implementing pulse-and-glide incorrectly creates traffic congestion, annoys other motorists, and introduces safety hazards. Adhere strictly to these four professional operating rules:

1. The Golden Rule of Lane Selection

Never execute pulse-and-glide in the left or passing lanes of multi-lane roads. Always remain in the right lane on four-lane divided arterials. If traveling on a two-lane undivided road and another vehicle approaches from behind, immediately abandon pulse-and-glide and maintain a steady cruising speed until the following driver turns off or safely passes.

2. The Tight Velocity Window (±5 to 7 MPH)

Do not fluctuate speed by extreme margins (such as 20 to 50 mph). Maintain a tight, predictable speed window of no more than 12 to 14 mph total delta (e.g., pulsing to 44 mph and gliding to 32 mph in a 40 mph zone). This modest speed oscillation mirrors the natural speed variations of surrounding commercial traffic and does not disrupt general traffic flow.

3. Brake Pedal Isolation

Never use friction brakes to regulate speed during a pulse-and-glide cycle. Touching the brake pedal wastes kinetic momentum and dumps thermal energy into the brake pads. If upcoming traffic forces you to brake, your glide window was miscalculated; resume steady-state driving until traffic clears.

4. Weather and Surface Restrictions

Never perform neutral gliding or throttle pulsing on wet, icy, or snow-covered pavement. Shifting into Neutral removes engine drag, which compromises stability control systems and electronic brake force distribution. Keep the transmission locked in "Drive" at all times during adverse weather.

⚠️ Never Turn the Ignition Off While Driving

Never turn off the vehicle ignition key or push-button start while coasting in a non-hybrid automobile ("Engine-Off Coasting"). Turning off the ignition disables hydraulic power steering, depletes brake vacuum booster reserves within two pedal presses, and risks locking the mechanical steering column lock. In modern non-hybrid cars, execute glides with the engine running at idle.

To maximize total system efficiency, combine pulse-and-glide with calibrated tire inflation pressures, optimize high-speed transit using highway speed sweet spot facts, manage elevation changes using our hilly terrain cruise control guide, and explore powertrain mechanics in hybrid powertrain operations inside our hypermiling knowledge hub.

faqs.question: Can I do pulse and glide in an automatic transmission without shifting to Neutral?
faqs.answer: Yes. You can execute pulse-and-glide in an automatic transmission simply by leaving the gear selector in Drive. Pulse briskly at 75% throttle up to 45 mph, then lift your foot completely off the accelerator to let the car glide in top overdrive gear under Deceleration Fuel Cut-Off (DFCO). While engine braking reduces glide distance compared to Neutral, DFCO consumes zero fuel and requires no shifter manipulation.

faqs.question: Does shifting an automatic transmission between Neutral and Drive while moving cause wear?
faqs.answer: No wear occurs if the transition is performed smoothly with the engine running. In a modern electronically controlled automatic transmission, shifting from N to D at 35 mph causes the transmission control module to match hydraulic line pressure and smoothly engage the forward clutch pack. Gently tapping the throttle to rev-match the engine before pulling the lever into D eliminates all clutch friction.

faqs.question: Why does pulse and glide work better in hybrids than conventional cars?
faqs.answer: Pulse-and-glide works better in hybrids because hybrid vehicles can completely shut down the gasoline engine during the glide phase, eliminating fuel consumption and engine friction entirely. In addition, power-split transmissions (e-CVT) allow electric motors to balance torque to zero, creating a frictionless freewheel glide that rolls twice as far as a conventional car.

faqs.question: Will pulse and glide ruin my vehicle starter or battery?
faqs.answer: In conventional cars where the engine remains idling during the glide, the starter motor and battery experience zero extra cycles. In hybrid vehicles, the internal combustion engine is restarted seamlessly by high-voltage motor-generator MG1 using the 200V+ traction battery, which is specifically engineered to handle hundreds of thousands of restart cycles without degradation.

faqs.question: Does pulse and glide work at highway speeds of 70 mph?
faqs.answer: Pulse-and-glide is ineffective at speeds above 65 mph because aerodynamic drag increases exponentially with the square of speed. At 70 mph, aerodynamic resistance causes the vehicle to decelerate rapidly during the glide, shortening the glide phase to a few seconds and eliminating any Brake Specific Fuel Consumption advantage.

faqs.question: Is pulse and glide legal on public roadways?
faqs.answer: Pulse-and-glide is completely legal on public roads as long as drivers maintain safe following distances, remain within posted speed limits, and do not impede traffic. Some jurisdictions have statutes prohibiting coasting in Neutral on steep mountain descents; drivers in those jurisdictions execute pulse-and-glide using in-gear DFCO gliding in Drive.
